> I've been pondering over exactly this problem before and I'm not sure what's the best way forward (mostly because I'm not very familiar with how shell completion works):

It can be written in two main styles (looking at bash):
1. Raw replies to shell - this is where you populate $COMPREPLY directly after parsing these local variables `cur prev words cword`. You can use that for complex syntax in a single argument. I wrote these in the past and I can't read them anymore :)
2. Using helpers "here are my keywords" - this is where `compgen` helpers fill in $COMPREPLY based on what args you pass it (-W for words, filedir for files, etc.)

> * Add lots of "pseudo options" like you suggested (I'm quite certain the two you mentioned are not sufficient — there are sub-options for the different compression algos, there are categories that depend on the configuration, ...). My gut feeling is that this is a bit messy.

Think of `git switch <TAB>` or `apt show gcc<TAB>` - for those, "user data", the completion calls the program at runtime. Here is [apt show](https://salsa.debian.org/apt-team/apt/-/blob/main/completions/bash/apt?ref_type=heads#L191) completion for example. And some pseudo options may be generally useful. For example, I didn't know 'lz4hc' existed.

On the other hand, if you mean "level" in `--schema-compression=zstd:level=16` -- that's kinda doable, similar to something like `git log HEAD..<TAB>` which knows about '..'. But I'd argue that that's pretty advanced completion. It could be done as part of "ls-comp-algos" where it prints a delimited list so you don't have too many pseudo options.

If your zstd options were a pass through (which I don't think they are), like zstd's strategy, windowLog, ..., then you would not complete those and instead send users to "zstd(1)" to browse other options and let the program validate at runtime.


> * Add a more formal JSON definition of the options/value supported. Seems a bit nicer, but probably too much overhead and I've no idea if/how the JSON could be used by shell-completion.

Completion needs the reply variable populated, so JSON would have to be parsed at shell runtime using something like `jq`. I would skip this idea.

> * Make the binary output the whole shell-completion config (`mkdwarfs bash-completion-config`). This seems like a good compromise: it's simpler than structured JSON (although not reusable), and likely more lightweight than calling the binary half a dozen times and then still having to parse the output.

This is a pretty good idea in general and very common in statically-linked langs. Most golang completions are really a [stub file](https://salsa.debian.org/debian/bash-completion/-/blob/master/completions/_golangci-lint) calling `<program> completion {bash,zsh}`. (try it with docker, glow, npm?). The completion script then calls `<program> __complete "...."` at runtime to get the actual commands/options list.

But golang has [cobra](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/main/bash_completionsV2.go) for that.

And still, they will be _calling the binary half a dozen times_ at runtime, I'm afraid :)

In any case, the completion script has to be there when the shell starts up, whether it does something significant or just a single `eval` call.


> One advantage of the last two options is that you can actually use `boost::program_options::options_description` to automatically collect information about most of the available options. Which means you don't have to maintain a set of options in two different places and (likely) have them go out of sync with a new release. (I've already added unit tests that ensure the actual command line options of a binary are in sync with the respective manpage...)

For statically linked langs, this is a must due to the 1-file heaven they live in. On the other hand, you have the advantage of installing files.

Using `program_options` could be done by
1. Asking the program to output the full completion script. But source would include ugly shell language in C++ strings, think lots of "\\"", (unless there is a boost equivalent to cobra?)
2. Asking the program to output a stub that calls the program at runtime. But it would need a dedicated `complete` option that can parse `cur prev words cword` args and replies with a valid list. (think receiving './<TAB>' and having to list files, listing users, etc., stuff which the shell is really good at)
3. Asking the program to list all options in plain text where the completion script transforms it and passes it to a helper. But you might lose some features unless you have "type" info (files, list of algos, etc..).

All those require that you have a working completion script first to be able to embed parts of it in C++.

Alternatively, you could:

4. Restructure `-H` to be more scriptable. You could list the compression algos with a prefix so they're easier to parse. Move the file hash algos to the bottom so they're easier to extract. Maybe later this can then be transformed from statically written completion to auto-generated at build time. I have a completion that parses `<program> --help` and looks for `<file>` and `<dir>` in the args to decide what comes next. But the completion and programs are written together carefully :)

In fact, thinking about it further, maybe pseudo options could all be skipped if `-H` updates a couple of parts. Can you list compression options there?

Anyway, as a user, IMHO, I *really* want to see a list of options and files most of all. Then it would be *nice* to see option arguments. Like "was it --loglevel or --log-level?" first, then if my "zstd" shows me ":level", then "oh, cool".

I would suggest separating this into steps:
1. Write a basic completion file, this is shell language. Skip all compile-dependent arguments and force the shell to be silent. So something like `--file-hash=<TAB>` says nothing, forcing the user to `-H` instead.
2. Figure out how to improve completions statically for a given build. This is the shell language itself with hard-coded hashes/compressions/categories/etc.
3. Decide on options 1 to 4 above based on complexity of 2.

Also maybe release the basic one and get some user feedback :)

> It can be written in two main styles (looking at bash):
> 
> 1. Raw replies to shell - this is where you populate $COMPREPLY directly after parsing these local variables `cur prev words cword`. You can use that for complex syntax in a single argument. I wrote these in the past and I can't read them anymore :)

:)

> > * Add a more formal JSON definition of the options/value supported. Seems a bit nicer, but probably too much overhead and I've no idea if/how the JSON could be used by shell-completion.
> 
> Completion needs the reply variable populated, so JSON would have to be parsed at shell runtime using something like `jq`. I would skip this idea.

That's fair (and what I already suspected).

> This is a pretty good idea in general and very common in statically-linked langs. Most golang completions are really a [stub file](https://salsa.debian.org/debian/bash-completion/-/blob/master/completions/_golangci-lint) calling `<program> completion {bash,zsh}`. (try it with docker, glow, npm?). The completion script then calls `<program> __complete "...."` at runtime to get the actual commands/options list.
> 
> But golang has [cobra](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/main/bash_completionsV2.go) for that.
> 
> And still, they will be _calling the binary half a dozen times_ at runtime, I'm afraid :)

Hahaha, too bad! :)

> Using `program_options` could be done by
> 
> 1. Asking the program to output the full completion script. But source would include ugly shell language in C++ strings, think lots of "\"", (unless there is a boost equivalent to cobra?)

True. Raw strings might help, but I agree it's probably nasty. I don't think there's anything like cobra for boost::po.

> 4. Restructure `-H` to be more scriptable. You could list the compression algos with a prefix so they're easier to parse. Move the file hash algos to the bottom so they're easier to extract. Maybe later this can then be transformed from statically written completion to auto-generated at build time. I have a completion that parses `<program> --help` and looks for `<file>` and `<dir>` in the args to decide what comes next. But the completion and programs are written together carefully :)

As far as I'm aware, there's not a lot of options regarding how boost::po formats the help output (but I may be wrong).

Moving the file hash algos to the bottom is certainly doable; it's hardly worse than listing them inline. :)

> In fact, thinking about it further, maybe pseudo options could all be skipped if `-H` updates a couple of parts. Can you list compression options there?

The compression options *are* already listed there:

```
Compression algorithms:
  null     no compression at all
  lzma     LZMA compression (liblzma 5.8.1)
               level=[0..9]
               dict_size=[12..30]
               extreme
               binary={arm, armthumb, ia64, powerpc, sparc, x86}
               mode={fast, normal}
               mf={bt2, bt3, bt4, hc3, hc4}
               nice=[0..273]
               depth=[0..4294967295]
  zstd     ZSTD compression (libzstd 1.5.7)
               level=[-131072..22]
  lz4      LZ4 compression (liblz4 1.10.0)
  lz4hc    LZ4 HC compression (liblz4 1.10.0)
               level=[0..12]
  brotli   Brotli compressor (encoder 1.1.0)
               quality=[0..11]
               lgwin=[10..30]
  flac     FLAC compression (libFLAC++ 1.5.0)
               level=[0..8]
               exhaustive
  ricepp   RICEPP compression
               block_size=[16..512]
```

> Anyway, as a user, IMHO, I _really_ want to see a list of options and files most of all. Then it would be _nice_ to see option arguments. Like "was it --loglevel or --log-level?" first, then if my "zstd" shows me ":level", then "oh, cool".

Definitely.

> I would suggest separating this into steps:
> 
> 1. Write a basic completion file, this is shell language. Skip all compile-dependent arguments and force the shell to be silent. So something like `--file-hash=<TAB>` says nothing, forcing the user to `-H` instead.
> 2. Figure out how to improve completions statically for a given build. This is the shell language itself with hard-coded hashes/compressions/categories/etc.
> 3. Decide on options 1 to 4 above based on complexity of 2.
> 
> Also maybe release the basic one and get some user feedback :)

Sounds good to me. As long as we avoid things like path completion not working where it should and the completion code re-writing parts that it doesn't understand (I've seen both happen with some completion scripts in the past and it's really annoying), I'm all for starting with a basic script and improving things over time.

This changes the public API of `ratio_to_string` from `(double, double, ...)` to `(uint64_t, uint64_t, ...)`, which is a breaking header change for downstream users and in-repo call sites that naturally produce floating-point ratios. Seeding the RNG with `__TIME__` makes the sampled subset non-deterministic between builds, which can lead to irreproducible failures and makes it harder to diagnose CI issues. `mi_version()` historically encodes the version as major*100 + minor*10 + patch (e.g. 2.1.7 -> 217). body: Please add yourself as an author (even if this is using one of the other compression implementations as a template).

I would prefer if this was done differently.

In the LZ4 code that this was likely taken from, I historically made the (admittedly questionably) choice to just throw a 32-bit int at the start to encode the size. This was long before thinking about supporting big-endian architectures (or even thinking about making DwarFS public).

Every compression algorithm that was added later and didn't encode the uncompressed size itself (e.g. brotli or flac) uses variable length (and byte-order independent) integers. See [here](https://github.com/mhx/dwarfs/blob/main/src/compression/brotli.cpp#L555-L563) and [here](https://github.com/mhx/dwarfs/blob/main/src/compression/brotli.cpp#L611) for example. I'd prefer if we'd change this code to also use `varint`.
I'd move this out into a private static method (`checked_subspan` or something like that) and use `DWARFS_THROW`. That keeps the initialization list a bit more readable.
Can you make this `explicit`? Otherwise `clang-tidy` will also complain.

`order` stores map iterators, but the `std::ranges::sort` projection `&T::value_type::first` is applied to the iterator itself, not to `*it`. This will not compile (or will be ill-formed) because the iterator type has no `first` member. Use a projection/lambda that returns the key from the iterator (e.g., `[](iterator it){ return it->first; }`) or store pointers/refs to `value_type` instead of iterators.

This change removes several previously-declared virtual methods (e.g., `path_as_string()`, `name()`, `size()`, `allocated_size()`) from a public header, which is an ABI/API breaking change for any downstream implementations/users of `entry_interface`. If the intent is to narrow the interface, consider either (1) introducing a new interface type and deprecating the old one, or (2) keeping the old methods with defaulted/redirected implementations until a major-version bump.

The comment is missing a negation and currently reads as the opposite of the likely intent. It should say that `clear` does *not* affect the allocated memory.
```suggestion
    // clear *only* resets the size and does not affect the allocated memory
```
